newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. apologises to Japan over misfired bullets.
newsitem.headline: U.S. apologises to Japan over misfired bullets.

text.p: The United States apologised on Monday for mistakenly firing 1,520 bullets containing depleted uranium during a military exercise on a southern Japanese island near Okinawa in late 1995 and early 1996.
"The U.S. government has told the government of Japan that it regrets these incidents and the late notification," the U.S. Forces in Japan said in a statement.
The Pentagon notified Tokyo about the incident only in mid-January, but the Pentagon spokesman said the U.S. government was not required to notify the Japanese unless there were health risks.
Japan, in its own statement, while accepting the apology, said it "regretted" that it took the United States over a year to advise Tokyo of the incident.
"We find the incident, as well as the fact that it took the U.S. this long to report the case, extremely regrettable," Vice Foreign Minister Sadayuki Hayashi told a news conference.

The incident comes at a sensitive time when Tokyo is in the midst of a dispute with Okinawa landlords over leases for land used by U.S. military bases. Forced leases for privately owned land in Okinawa expire on May 14.

Hayashi apologised for the delay in notifying Okinawa about the incident, explaining that the United States had already found the bullets to be safe and that Tokyo wanted to collect more information before making the incident public.
The disclosure comes after Washington and Tokyo agreed in December to thrash out a joint scheme to exchange information quickly on accidents involving U.S. military forces here.
An expert U.S. team had assessed the environmental and health impact of the accidental use of the radioactive bullets and found there were no health or environmental risks.

The depleted uranium helps the bullets pierce armour such as on tanks. Each of the 25 mm projectiles contained 5.2 ounces (147 grams) of depleted uranium, a heavy metal with about the same toxicity as lead.

A U.S. contractor recovered 192 of the bullets during a March 1996 cleanup, and Japan will conduct its own research to determine the incident's impact on the environment and whether there was a need for further clean-up efforts, Hayashi said.

The level of radioactivity measured on Tori Shima, an isolated gunnery range 90 km (55 miles) from Okinawa, was reported to be 10 times less than the level under which the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission would require a cleanup plan.
The ammunition was intended for use only in combat or live-fire exercises in the United States. It was not to be used on Okinawa under a U.S.-Japanese agreement.
The U.S. statement said the 25 mm bullets were "improperly catalogued".

The Okinawan antipathy to the U.S. bases, which occupy about one-fifth of the land of the sub-tropical island, exploded in September 1995 after the rape of a local schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen.
The three are serving prison sentences for the crime.
